title: Key hierarchy and the HSM
summary: See how envelope encryption keeps a stored secret useless without KMS access.

blocks.text: 1Claw encrypts every secret with envelope encryption. A random 256-bit DEK encrypts the value with AES-256-GCM, then a per-vault KEK that never leaves the HSM wraps the DEK. In production the HSM is Google Cloud KMS at FIPS 140-2 Level 3 protection.

items: JWT signing key: one Ed25519 key per deployment, in the same KMS key ring
KEK: one symmetric key per vault, wraps and unwraps DEKs
DEK: fresh 256-bit key per secret version, never persisted in the clear
KEKs rotate on a 365-day period; KMS keeps old versions for decrypt

blocks.text: Every KMS encrypt, decrypt, and sign includes a CRC32C checksum. If the checksum mismatches in transit, the operation fails immediately instead of returning corrupt data.

steps.text: Exchange your API key for a bearer token. Replace 1ck_your_key_here with your real key from Settings → API Keys.
steps.code:
export ONECLAW_API_KEY="1ck_your_key_here"
export TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/auth/api-key-token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"api_key\":\"$ONECLAW_API_KEY\"}" | jq -r .access_token)

steps.text: Use your vault UUID from `1claw vault list` or Foundations.

Store a secret. Use a 1ck_ user key (which has full access), or an agent JWT with a write policy on this path. On the wire this is plaintext; at rest 1Claw generates a DEK, encrypts the value, and wraps the DEK with the vault KEK.

Read the secret back. The API returns the decrypted value; reason about what is stored at rest vs. returned in memory. The database holds only ciphertext, the wrapped DEK, IV, and tag. Without a KMS unwrap none of it decrypts.

blocks.text: You stored a secret and can now explain why a stolen database is worthless: the plaintext DEK exists only in memory during the operation, and the KEK never leaves the HSM.
Where this goes wrong in practice. The hierarchy is simple enough to draw on a whiteboard, and almost every failure comes from a gap between the drawing and the deployment.

items: The application caches decrypted material. An HSM call has latency, so someone adds a cache, and the plaintext DEK now lives in process memory for the lifetime of the pod. The key never left the HSM and the secret is readable from a core dump.
The audit log is treated as a byproduct. Non-exportability means misuse is your detection surface, so an HSM log nobody ships anywhere converts your best forensic record into a file that ages out.
Key versions are pruned to tidy up. Rotation creates a version and old data still points at the old one. Deleting retired versions is cryptographic erasure performed by accident.
The credential that calls the HSM is treated as ordinary. It is the whole boundary. A key file on disk is protected by the HSM; the token that authorises calls to it usually is not.

blocks.text: The pattern across all four: the hardware boundary is strong and everything adjacent to it is ordinary software. Attackers do not attack the boundary, they attack what stands next to it.

blocks.situation: An engineer reports that an attacker briefly had shell on an application server. That server does not hold key material; it authenticates to the HSM and calls it to sign and unwrap. Access was revoked after roughly forty minutes.
blocks.question: What is the correct assessment of the damage?

options.text: The keys are safe because they never left the HSM, so no action is needed.
options.feedback: Half right, and the dangerous half is missing. Non-exportability means the attacker could not take the key with them, which is a real containment win. But for forty minutes they could ask the HSM to perform operations, and it would have complied. You have to establish what was signed or decrypted in that window.

options.text: Assume every operation the server could request was performed, audit the HSM log for that window, and rotate anything the results touched.
options.feedback: Correct. An HSM protects against key theft, not key misuse. The key is intact, so you do not need to re-key the hierarchy, but every operation in that window is suspect and the audit log is the only record of what actually happened.

options.text: Rotate the KEK immediately and re-wrap every DEK.
options.feedback: Disproportionate, and it treats the wrong risk. The KEK was never exposed, so rotating it costs real effort and fixes nothing. Rotation is the answer to key compromise; this was credential compromise.

options.text: Destroy the HSM key version so anything signed during the window becomes invalid.
options.feedback: This confuses signing with encryption. Destroying a key version makes data encrypted under it unreadable, but it does not retroactively invalidate signatures already produced and accepted by others. You would also lose access to legitimate data.

quiz.question: What wraps the DEK before it is stored?
options: The per-vault KEK inside the HSM
quiz.explanation: The per-vault KEK, inside the HSM. One KEK per vault rather than one per system is what keeps a compromise scoped to a single vault instead of the whole store.

quiz.question: What FIPS level is the production HSM?
quiz.explanation: FIPS 140-2 Level 3, which requires tamper-evidence and identity-based operator authentication. It is the level most compliance regimes ask for by name, so it is worth being able to state.

quiz.question: How often do KEKs rotate automatically?
quiz.explanation: Every 365 days, which is the NIST SP 800-57 maximum for a symmetric KEK rather than an arbitrary interval. Old versions stay available, because data encrypted under them still needs to be readable.

title: Lab: the key hierarchy under compromise
summary: Build a KEK and DEK tree, take a shell on the application server, then rotate the KEK and watch it change nothing.

blocks.text: The key hierarchy lesson claimed that an HSM protects against key theft rather than key misuse, and that the audit log is therefore your detection surface rather than a byproduct. This lab puts an attacker inside the boundary that claim is about.
Each step appends to the same script, so every run reprints the sections before it. The expected output shown under each step is the new part; scroll to the bottom of your terminal to find it.

steps.text: Build the hierarchy. The HSM object holds the KEK and never returns it, exactly as real non-exportability works; the application server holds ciphertext and wrapped DEKs.
Now put an attacker on the application server. They cannot take the KEK, because it is not there to take.
steps.code:
cat >> hsm.py <<'EOF'

print("\n--- attacker has a shell on the app server ---")
print("steal the KEK? ", "no, it never leaves the HSM")
print("read a secret? ", read_secret("stripe/key", "app-server(attacker)").decode())
EOF
python3 hsm.py

steps.text: The key is safe and the secret is not.
steps.code:
--- attacker has a shell on the app server ---
steal the KEK?  no, it never leaves the HSM
read a secret?  sk-live-9f2a

steps.text: Do the thing everyone reaches for in an incident: rotate the KEK and re-wrap every DEK.
steps.code:
cat >> hsm.py <<'EOF'

print("\n--- incident response: rotate the KEK ---")
old = hsm.rotate()
for e in STORE.values():
    dek = xor(e["wrapped_dek"], old)
    e["wrapped_dek"] = xor(dek, hsm._kek)
print("rotated, all DEKs re-wrapped.")
print("attacker still on the box:", read_secret("stripe/key", "app-server(attacker)").decode())
EOF
python3 hsm.py

steps.text: Rotation completed successfully and achieved nothing, because the attacker was never using the key material. They were using the ability to ask.
steps.code:
--- incident response: rotate the KEK ---
rotated, all DEKs re-wrapped.
attacker still on the box: sk-live-9f2a

steps.text: Look at what does tell you something.
steps.code:
cat >> hsm.py <<'EOF'

print("\n--- the HSM audit log ---")
for entry in hsm.log:
    print("   ", entry)
EOF
python3 hsm.py

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: Three conclusions, and the second is the one that changes how you run an incident.

items: Non-exportability worked exactly as advertised. The attacker could not take the key with them, so their access ended when their access ended, and nothing was compromised permanently.

Rotation was the wrong response. It is the reflex for key compromise, and this was credential compromise. The effective action is revoking whatever let the attacker call the HSM, which in production is the token or certificate the application authenticates with.
The log is the only record of what actually happened. Every unwrap is there, attributed to a caller. Without it you would know an attacker had access and nothing about what they did with it.

blocks.text: This is why the credential that calls the HSM deserves the same care as key material. The key file is protected by hardware; the token authorising calls to it usually sits in an environment variable.

In an incident, ask what the attacker was actually using. If they held key material, rotate. If they held the ability to invoke, revoke the invoker and read the log to scope the damage. Rotating in the second case burns hours and changes nothing.

quiz.question: Why did rotating the KEK not stop the attacker?
options: They were using the ability to call the HSM, not the key material
quiz.explanation: Rotation is the response to key compromise. This was credential compromise, so the effective action is revoking whatever authorises calls to the HSM.

quiz.question: What did non-exportability actually achieve here?
options: It prevented the secrets from being read
The attacker could not take the key away, so their capability ended with their access
quiz.explanation: The blast radius is bounded in time rather than eliminated. A stolen key file works forever and anywhere; this attacker lost everything the moment their access was revoked.

quiz.question: What is the practical consequence for the credential the application uses to call the HSM?
options: It is the actual boundary and deserves the same care as key material
It only matters for audit attribution
It should be stored alongside the wrapped DEKs
It can be long-lived because the HSM is the real control
quiz.explanation: The key is protected by hardware and the token authorising its use frequently is not, which makes that token the weakest link in an otherwise strong hierarchy.

title: Customer-managed keys (CMEK)
summary: Add a client-side AES-256-GCM layer so 1Claw stores only your key's fingerprint.

blocks.text: CMEK double-encrypts secrets. You encrypt the value with your own AES-256-GCM key in the browser or your process, then 1Claw applies its HSM envelope encryption on top. Your key never touches the server; only its SHA-256 fingerprint is stored so the vault knows which key was used. CMEK is available on Business and Enterprise plans.
The client-side wire format is one version byte (0x01), a 12-byte IV, the ciphertext, then a 16-byte GCM auth tag. A full server compromise yields only doubly-encrypted blobs.
Requires a Business or Enterprise plan. CMEK changes who can decrypt your data, so it is gated at the tier where that trade is usually a contractual requirement rather than a preference.

steps.text: Install the SDK and have an API key ready.
Export your API key and vault ID. Replace with your real values from Settings → API Keys and `1claw vault list`.
Exchange your API key for a bearer token.
Save the code below as `cmek-demo.ts`. It generates a 256-bit key, encrypts a secret, stores it, reads it back, and decrypts it. Store the key safely because you need it for every read and write.
Copy the fingerprint value printed above into the curl body below. Enable CMEK on the vault by sending only the fingerprint.

blocks.text: To rotate, send the old and new keys to POST /v1/vaults/:id/cmek-rotate. The server re-encrypts in batches of 100, atomically per batch, and holds both keys in memory only for the duration of the job.
The vault now requires your key for every value, and 1Claw cannot decrypt your secrets unilaterally.

Two easy mistakes here. generateCmekKey, cmekFingerprint, cmekEncrypt and cmekDecrypt all return promises, so every one needs await. And cmekEncrypt takes (plaintext, key) in that order, both as Uint8Array: swapping them produces a blob that will never decrypt.
Where this goes wrong in practice. CMEK moves a real risk from the provider to the customer, and the failures are consistently operational rather than cryptographic.

items: No escrow. The most common CMEK incident is not theft, it is a laptop and an unrecoverable vault. Enrolment should be paired with a customer-controlled escrow before the first secret is written.

Rotation is started and never finished. Server-assisted rotation runs in batches with progress tracking, and a job interrupted midway leaves secrets split across two keys. Both keys must be retained until the job reports completion.
The fingerprint is mistaken for a backup. It is a SHA-256 of the key, which can verify a candidate but cannot reconstruct one. Teams have discovered this at exactly the wrong moment.

Client-side encryption is bypassed by one integration. A single service that writes through the API without encrypting first leaves plaintext in a vault everyone believes is customer-encrypted, and nothing in the interface will point it out.

blocks.text: The last one is worth auditing for directly. Uniform CMEK is a property of every writer, and it fails silently the moment one of them does not participate.

blocks.situation: A customer on CMEK reports that their finance team lost the laptop holding the only copy of their key. They have their dashboard login and their secrets are all still listed in the vault.
blocks.question: What can you actually do for them?

options.text: Restore the key from the server-side backup taken at enrolment.
options.feedback: There is no such backup, and that is the point of CMEK. Only the SHA-256 fingerprint is stored server-side, which can verify a key but cannot reconstruct one.

options.text: Nothing recovers the values. The ciphertext is unreadable, and they must re-supply every secret under a new key.
options.feedback: Correct, and it is the trade they accepted. The key never left their device, so the provider genuinely cannot help. This is why CMEK enrolment should be paired with an escrow process the customer controls.

options.text: Use server-assisted rotation to move the secrets onto a new key.
options.feedback: Rotation re-encrypts by decrypting with the old key first. Without that key there is nothing to rotate from. The feature helps you change keys, not recover from losing one.

options.text: Read the values from the audit log, which records secret access.
options.feedback: The audit log records that an access occurred, along with who and when. It never records the value; if it did, it would be a second copy of every secret in a place with weaker controls.

quiz.question: What does 1Claw store about your CMEK key?
options: An encrypted copy in the HSM
quiz.explanation: Only the SHA-256 fingerprint is stored so the vault can track which key was used.

quiz.question: What algorithm does the client-side CMEK layer use?
quiz.explanation: AES-256-GCM, applied client-side before the value is ever sent. GCM authenticates as well as encrypts, so a tampered ciphertext fails to decrypt rather than producing plausible garbage.

quiz.question: What protects a secret if the CMEK vault's database is stolen?
options: It is doubly encrypted and useless without your key
Only the fingerprint is needed to decrypt
quiz.explanation: Two independent layers, so a stolen backup yields doubly-encrypted blobs. The provider cannot decrypt it either, which is the trade you accepted: no provider access also means no provider recovery.

title: Lab: lose the key and find out what that means
summary: Encrypt client-side, hand the server only a fingerprint, then delete your key and try every recovery path.

blocks.text: The CMEK lesson said the provider cannot help you if the key is lost, and that the fingerprint verifies rather than reconstructs. Those are load-bearing claims for a feature people enable to satisfy an auditor, so they are worth checking rather than accepting.

steps.text: Model the split: the customer holds the key, the server holds ciphertext and a fingerprint.
steps.code:
cat > /tmp/cmek.py <<'EOF'
import os, hashlib
xor = lambda a, b: bytes(x ^ y for x, y in zip(a, b * (len(a)//len(b) + 1)))

key = os.urandom(32)                       # never leaves the customer
fingerprint = hashlib.sha256(key).hexdigest()
blob = xor(b"sk-live-9f2a", key)           # encrypted before upload

print("server stores fingerprint:", fingerprint[:16], "...")
print("server stores ciphertext: ", blob.hex()[:24], "...")

# the fingerprint can confirm a candidate key
candidate = key
print("\nfingerprint verifies a candidate:",
      hashlib.sha256(candidate).hexdigest() == fingerprint)

# ... and cannot produce one
del key, candidate
try:
    print(xor(blob, key))
except NameError:
    print("customer lost the key -> unrecoverable, by design")
EOF
python3 /tmp/cmek.py

steps.text: The fingerprint did exactly one useful thing and could not do the other. Your fingerprint and ciphertext will differ from these, because the key is generated fresh on every run; the two lines that matter are the last two.
steps.code:
server stores fingerprint: 6b16b6d49124d0b4 ...
server stores ciphertext:  9923abb66f8a4e11c284ad76 ...

fingerprint verifies a candidate: True
customer lost the key -> unrecoverable, by design

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: A SHA-256 of the key can confirm that a key you already have is the right one. It cannot run backwards, so it is a checksum rather than an escrow, and no amount of provider goodwill changes that.

items: Verification is the fingerprint's whole job: it lets the server reject a wrong key before wasting a decryption attempt.
There is no server-side copy by construction. That is the property being purchased, and its cost is that recovery is your problem.
Server-assisted rotation decrypts with the old key first, so it is not a recovery path either. Losing the key means losing the ability to rotate as well as to read.

blocks.text: Pair every CMEK enrolment with a customer-controlled escrow before the first secret is written. Split the key across two safes, put it in a hardware token with a documented successor, do something. The most common CMEK incident is not an attacker, it is a laptop.

This is the same trade as the client-custody MPC modes, one step further. Stronger guarantees against the provider always mean weaker guarantees against yourself, and the decision belongs to whoever will be answering for both.

quiz.question: What can the stored fingerprint do?
options: Confirm that a candidate key is the right one, and nothing more
Prove the key was generated correctly
Reconstruct the key if the customer loses it
quiz.explanation: A hash runs one way. It is a checksum that saves a wasted decryption attempt, not an escrow, and expecting otherwise is the misunderstanding that turns a lost laptop into lost data.

quiz.question: Why is server-assisted rotation not a recovery path?
options: It rotates the fingerprint rather than the key
It decrypts with the old key first, so losing the key loses rotation too
It only works on vaults under 100 secrets
quiz.explanation: Rotation re-encrypts from plaintext it must first obtain. Without the old key there is nothing to rotate from, so the loss takes both capabilities.

quiz.question: What should accompany every CMEK enrolment?
options: A second vault with the same secrets
A customer-controlled escrow, established before the first secret is written
A support contract with recovery SLAs
quiz.explanation: The provider genuinely cannot help, so the recovery plan has to be yours and has to exist before it is needed. The common CMEK incident is a lost laptop, not an attacker.

title: MPC secret storage
summary: Split a secret's DEK across parties so no single holder can reconstruct it.

blocks.text: MPC splits each secret's DEK into shares so one compromised holder cannot decrypt. It layers on top of the standard HSM envelope encryption and is set per vault. The custody mode is immutable once set.

items: 2of2_client_custody: XOR split between the server HSM and you; you hold a client_share
2of3_multi_hsm: Shamir 2-of-3 across GCP, AWS, and Azure; no client share
2of3_client_custody: Shamir 2-of-3 with two HSMs plus your client share

blocks.text: For client-custody modes, store the client_share safely. Lose it on a 2of2_client_custody vault and the secret cannot be recovered, because the server holds only its single share.
Create a dedicated vault for MPC testing; custody mode cannot be changed after it is set.
Requires a Pro or higher plan. Custody mode is also immutable once set on a vault, so create a throwaway vault to experiment with rather than deciding on a real one.

steps.text: Export your API key and vault ID. Use your vault UUID from `1claw vault list` or Foundations.
Exchange your API key for a bearer token.
Enable MPC with XOR client custody. This choice is permanent for the vault.
Write a secret. The PUT response includes a base64 client_share you must keep. Capture it from the response.
steps.code:
RESPONSE=$(curl -s -X PUT https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$VAULT_ID/secrets/api-keys/stripe \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"value":"sk_live_abc123","type":"api_key"}')
CLIENT_SHARE=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | jq -r .client_share)
echo "Save this client_share permanently: $CLIENT_SHARE"

steps.text: Read it back by sending your share in X-Client-Share. Without the header the read fails.

blocks.text: The vault now returns a client_share on write and requires it on read, so 1Claw alone cannot reconstruct the DEK.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Threshold schemes are mathematically sound and operationally demanding, and the gap between those two is where incidents live.

items: Custody mode is immutable, and it is chosen early. The decision is made during a spike, by whoever is setting up the vault, usually before anyone has thought about who will hold a share in a year.
The client share has no owner. A share held by "the team" is held by nobody. It needs a named custodian, a documented location, and a successor.

The X-Client-Share header is forgotten in one path. Client-custody modes require it on every read, and the service that was written last, or by a different team, is the one that discovers this in production.

Availability is confused with security. 2-of-3 tolerates losing one share; 2-of-2 tolerates nothing. Teams pick 2-of-2 for its stronger trust property and discover the availability cost during an incident.

blocks.text: Before enabling a client-custody mode, write down who holds the share, where, and who takes over if they leave. If that is hard to answer, choose multi-HSM instead: a weaker trust assumption you can operate beats a stronger one you cannot.

blocks.situation: You are choosing a custody mode for a vault holding the signing material behind a treasury that moves large sums. The team is small and operationally inexperienced, and there is no formal key-escrow process.
blocks.question: Which mode fits, and why?

options.text: 2of2_client_custody, so the provider mathematically cannot act alone.
options.feedback: The trust property is exactly what you want, but pair it with this team and it is a liability. Both shares are required, one is held by them, and losing it is unrecoverable. Strong cryptography plus weak key operations is how funds get permanently locked, not secured.

options.text: 2of3_multi_hsm, so no single HSM provider holds a complete key and losing one share is survivable.
options.feedback: Correct for this team. It removes single-provider trust, which is the threat that matters here, while tolerating the loss of one share. Client custody is stronger against a colluding provider, but only if the client can actually operate a key.

options.text: No MPC. Standard envelope encryption in the HSM is enough for a treasury.
options.feedback: Defensible for most vaults, but this one concentrates unusual value in a single provider's control. That is precisely the case where splitting custody earns its operational cost.

options.text: 2of3_client_custody, for the strongest guarantee available.
options.feedback: It is the strongest, and it still requires this team to hold and never lose a share. Choosing the maximum guarantee without the operational maturity to support it trades a modest risk for a catastrophic one.

quiz.question: Which mode returns a client_share and needs X-Client-Share on reads?
quiz.explanation: 2of2_client_custody splits by XOR and hands you one share, which must be presented as X-Client-Share on every read. That is the strongest trust property available and the least forgiving: lose the share and the secret is gone.

quiz.question: Can a vault's MPC custody mode be changed after it is set?
quiz.explanation: Immutable once set, which is why the mode should be chosen deliberately rather than during a spike. Changing your mind means creating a new vault and migrating the secrets into it.

quiz.question: Where are the shares stored in 2of3_multi_hsm?
quiz.explanation: Three Shamir shares across GCP KMS, AWS KMS and Azure Key Vault. Spreading them across providers is the point: no single vendor, subpoena or outage reaches a complete key.

concepts.note: Shamir sharing and why MPC goes further

title: Shroud TEE proxy
summary: Route a chat completion through Shroud so it is inspected inside a hardware TEE.

blocks.text: Shroud is an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy running inside a confidential GKE node with AMD SEV-SNP. Your agent sends chat completions to Shroud instead of the provider. Shroud authenticates the agent, resolves the provider key, runs threat detection and secret redaction, then forwards the request. Secrets never leave your infrastructure in the clear.

items: Endpoint: POST https://shroud.1claw.co/v1/chat/completions
X-Shroud-Agent-Key: agent_id:api_key (the agent's ocv_ key)
X-Shroud-Provider: openai, anthropic, google, gemini, and others
Secret redaction, PII detection, and prompt-injection scoring run before the model sees the prompt

blocks.text: Prompt injection is scored 0.0 to 1.0. Anything above 0.9 is a hard block regardless of the agent's configured threshold, which defaults to 0.7.

steps.text: Set your agent credentials. Replace with your agent_id from agent creation and your ocv_ key from the agent's settings page.
Quick start: pass your provider key directly via X-Shroud-Api-Key. For production, store the key in the vault at providers/openai/api-key and grant the agent read access instead.
Parse the response. It follows the standard OpenAI shape.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://shroud.1claw.co/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "X-Shroud-Agent-Key: $ONECLAW_AGENT_ID:$ONECLAW_AGENT_API_KEY" \
  -H "X-Shroud-Provider: openai" \
  -H "X-Shroud-Api-Key: sk-your-openai-key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}' | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content'

blocks.text: No editor supports the X-Shroud headers natively. Run npx @1claw/cli proxy locally to bridge Cursor, Claude Code, and Copilot traffic into Shroud.
Your agent's LLM traffic now flows through the TEE proxy, inspected and redacted, with a normal OpenAI-style response coming back.
Where this goes wrong in practice. A TEE proxy is easy to deploy and easy to hold wrongly, because it produces a strong feeling of safety that outruns what it actually guarantees.

items: Attestation is enabled but never verified. The hardware signs a measurement of what loaded; if nothing on your side checks that measurement against an expected value, you have the ceremony without the assurance.

One caller bypasses the proxy. Unless intents_require_tee or execution_require_tee is set, direct API calls still work, and the service written before the proxy existed keeps using the path it always used.

Redaction is assumed to be complete. Inspection catches known secret values and recognisable patterns. A credential in a format it has never seen passes through, which is why the proxy is a layer rather than a guarantee.
Latency pressure erodes it. Every referral, prompt or completion pays the proxy cost, and the first performance review proposes a fast path around it for "internal" traffic.

blocks.text: Attestation proves which code is running. It does not prove that code is correct, and a faithfully attested enclave running a flawed program is flawed with a signature attached.

blocks.situation: An agent has intents_require_tee set. A developer reports that their new service calls the Intents API directly at api.1claw.co and receives a 403, and asks you to disable the flag so they can ship.
blocks.question: What is the right response?

options.text: Disable intents_require_tee for that agent, since the call is coming from your own infrastructure.
options.feedback: This is the reasoning the flag exists to prevent. The guarantee is not that the caller is trustworthy, it is that signing is routed through an attested enclave. Turning it off because a trusted service is inconvenienced removes the property for every caller, trusted or not.

options.text: Route the service through shroud.1claw.co instead, which is what the flag requires.
options.feedback: Correct. The 403 is the control working as designed. Shroud sets an HMAC-signed X-1Claw-TEE-Origin header that the Vault verifies, so the fix is to send the request through the enclave rather than to remove the requirement.

options.text: Add the service's IP to an allowlist so it can bypass the check.
options.feedback: The check is not about network origin, so an IP allowlist cannot satisfy it. It verifies a shared-secret HMAC header that only Shroud can produce, precisely so that reaching the API from a permitted address is not sufficient.

options.text: Give the service a second agent identity without the flag set.
options.feedback: This is the flag disabled with extra steps, and it is worse: you now have two identities for one workload, one of which quietly lacks the control, and the audit trail no longer tells you which path a signature took.

quiz.question: What is the format of the X-Shroud-Agent-Key header value?
quiz.explanation: Exactly agent_id:api_key, with the ocv_ key on the right. Shroud uses it to authenticate the agent before deciding what the request is allowed to reach.

quiz.question: At what prompt-injection score does Shroud hard-block regardless of config?
quiz.explanation: Above 0.9 is always blocked, whatever the agent's configured threshold. A hard ceiling exists so that a permissive per-agent setting cannot disable the control entirely.

quiz.question: What TEE technology runs the Shroud proxy?
quiz.explanation: AMD SEV-SNP on confidential GKE nodes, which encrypts VM memory so the host operator cannot read it. That is what makes inspecting sensitive prompts acceptable rather than merely centralised.

concepts.note: attestation and what it does not prove
what the proxy is inspecting for

title: Lab: change one line and fail attestation
summary: Compute a measurement, verify it, then add a harmless comment and watch the enclave refuse to be trusted.

blocks.text: The TEE lesson said attestation proves which code is running and does not prove that code is correct. Both halves of that sentence become obvious once you compute a measurement yourself.

steps.text: Measure some enclave code, pin the expected value, then try three builds against it.
steps.code:
cat > /tmp/att.py <<'EOF'
import hashlib
measure = lambda code: hashlib.sha256(code.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

GOOD = "def handle(req): return inspect(req)"
EXPECTED = measure(GOOD)
print(f"expected measurement: {EXPECTED}\n")

builds = [
    ("unchanged",      GOOD),
    ("added a comment", GOOD + "\n# log timings to /tmp"),
    ("attacker build",  "def handle(req): send(req, 'attacker'); return inspect(req)"),
]
for name, code in builds:
    m = measure(code)
    print(f"  {name:16} {m}  {'ACCEPT' if m == EXPECTED else 'REJECT'}")
EOF
python3 /tmp/att.py

steps.text: The attacker build is refused, and so is the comment.
steps.code:
expected measurement: b8462090a54460e2

  unchanged        b8462090a54460e2  ACCEPT
  added a comment  af45f9826b9edea7  REJECT
  attacker build   f8d52695a828d60d  REJECT

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: The mechanism cannot tell the difference between those two rejections, and that is the correct behaviour rather than a limitation. A measurement answers one question exactly: is this bit-for-bit the thing I expected.

items: Attestation is an equality check against a value you chose. Everything depends on that expected value being right, and nothing about the hardware helps you decide what it should be.
It says nothing about whether the code is any good. A carefully attested enclave running a flawed program is flawed with a signature attached.
Every legitimate deployment changes the measurement, so the expected value has to be updated with each release. That update is the moment the whole scheme can be quietly subverted.

blocks.text: That last point is where attestation goes wrong in practice. Nobody attacks the hardware; they get a new expected value accepted, through a build pipeline that publishes it or a process where updating it is routine and unreviewed.
The useful question is not whether attestation is enabled. It is who decides the expected measurement, how that decision is reviewed, and what would happen if someone changed it.

quiz.question: Why was the harmless comment rejected?
options: A measurement is a bit-for-bit equality check, so any change produces a different value
quiz.explanation: It answers exactly one question: is this identical to what I expected. It has no notion of a change being harmless.

quiz.question: What does a valid attestation not tell you?
options: Whether that code is correct or free of flaws
quiz.explanation: A faithfully attested enclave running a flawed program is flawed with a signature attached. Attestation is about identity, not quality.

quiz.question: Where does attestation usually fail in practice?
options: In how the expected measurement gets updated on each release
quiz.explanation: Every legitimate deploy changes the measurement, so updating the expected value is routine. Routine and unreviewed is exactly where an attacker prefers to work.

title: Zero trust and the risk engine
summary: Plant a honeytoken canary so any read trips a critical verdict and revokes sessions.

blocks.text: 1Claw assumes no implicit trust. Every request is authenticated, authorized against policy, and audited to a tamper-evident SHA-256 hash chain. Revocation is immediate: delete a policy and access stops on the next request. On top of that, the risk engine scores every authentication event in real time.

items: Geo-velocity: impossible travel between two locations
First-seen: a new ASN, country, or device for this principal
Honeytokens: decoy secrets whose access records a critical verdict
DPoP binds a JWT to a client keypair (RFC 9449)

blocks.text: A critical verdict triggers Continuous Access Evaluation: all of that principal's active tokens are revoked, their JTIs are added to the revoked list, and their next request fails auth. Verdicts carry a 15-minute TTL.

steps.text: Export your API key and vault ID. Use your vault UUID from `1claw vault list` or Foundations.
Exchange your API key for a bearer token.
Create a honeytoken. The honeytoken registers a canary on this path. Any read of this path triggers a critical alert and session revocation. Pick a path that looks valuable so an attacker is tempted.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/risk/honeytokens \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"vault_id":"'"$VAULT_ID"'","secret_path":"api-keys/production","notes":"Canary for vault breach"}'

steps.text: Confirm it is armed by listing your honeytokens.
Optional: read the honeytoken path and confirm the token is revoked on the next request.
steps.code:
curl -s https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$VAULT_ID/secrets/api-keys/production \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# Now try another request; it should fail with 401
curl -s https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$VAULT_ID/secrets/api-keys/production \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

blocks.text: When a honeytoken is read, the current request is not blocked so the attacker is not tipped off. Their next authentication attempt is denied instead.
You now have a live canary: any read of api-keys/production records a critical verdict and revokes that principal's sessions.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Zero trust fails less from bad architecture than from the slow accumulation of individually reasonable exceptions.

items: Grants outlive their reason. Access is added for a migration, the migration ends, and nothing removes it. Expiry on the grant is the only mechanism that survives people forgetting.

Least privilege is applied once, at creation. Scope is set carefully on day one and then only ever widened, because widening unblocks someone and narrowing risks breaking something nobody has time to test.
Break-glass becomes routine. An emergency path used twice a year is a control; used twice a month it is the normal path with extra logging.
Blast radius is never actually calculated. Teams assert that a compromise would be contained without enumerating what one credential reaches. The enumeration is usually surprising.

blocks.text: A useful exercise: pick your most ordinary service credential and list every resource it can reach today. Do it before an incident forces the same list under time pressure.

blocks.situation: A nightly reconciliation job has used the same 1ck_ key for two years. It works, nobody has touched it, and there has been no incident.
blocks.question: What is the strongest argument for changing it?

options.text: It has probably been copied somewhere by now, so it should be rotated on principle.
options.feedback: Plausible but unfalsifiable, and it will lose to 'if it isn't broken' every time. It also suggests rotation as the fix when the durable problem is duration itself.

options.text: A credential with no expiry converts any single past leak into permanent access, so the fix is a short-lived token rather than a fresher long-lived one.
options.feedback: Correct, and it is the argument that actually changes the design. Rotation resets the clock; expiry removes the property that makes a leak permanent. Exchange the key for a short-lived JWT at the point of use.

options.text: Two years exceeds most compliance rotation windows, so it is an audit finding.
options.feedback: Often true and useful for getting the work scheduled, but it argues from policy rather than risk, and it is satisfied by rotating to another two-year key.

options.text: The job should use mTLS instead, which does not expire.
options.feedback: Certificates do expire, and swapping the credential type without shortening its life leaves the same standing-access problem in a different format.

quiz.question: What does the audit log use to stay tamper-evident?
quiz.explanation: Audit entries form a SHA-256 hash chain, and inserts go through a SECURITY DEFINER function.

quiz.question: What happens the moment a honeytoken is read?
options: Nothing until a human reviews it
A critical verdict is recorded but the request proceeds
quiz.explanation: The read is allowed to avoid tipping off the attacker, but a critical verdict blocks their next auth.

quiz.question: What does DPoP protect against?
options: Use of a stolen JWT without the matching private key
quiz.explanation: DPoP binds a JWT to a client keypair, so a stolen token is useless without the private key.

title: Human Factor Auth for treasury
summary: Require a password or passkey from a real person before a treasury wallet can send, swap, or export.

blocks.text: Human Factor Auth (HFA, v0.56) puts a person in the loop on the operations that move money. Treasury wallet send, swap, and export can each require a password or a passkey before they proceed: regardless of what token the caller holds.
The policy resolves in a fixed order, most specific first:

items: The user's own human_factor_auth_policies.
Then human_factor_auth on the relevant wallet_spend_policies.
Then the system defaults.

blocks.text: HFA is about proving a human is present. It is deliberately separate from the agent guardrails in the Transactions track, which bound what an agent may attempt in the first place.

steps.text: Read the current policy.
Require a passkey for sends and exports, and a password for swaps.
Clients can prefetch the effective policy so they know which step-up to prompt for before the user hits send.
Satisfy the step-up. Mint a re-auth token, then present it on the protected call.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/auth/reauth/begin \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"method":"passkey"}'
# complete the ceremony, then send the resulting rat_ token:
#   -H "X-Auth-Confirm: rat_..."

blocks.text: Two webhooks make HFA observable: human_factor_auth.satisfied and human_factor_auth.denied. A run of denials is a strong signal that something is trying to move funds without a human.
Social-login users may have no password. If you require the password method they cannot satisfy it: have them enrol a passkey or TOTP at /settings/security first.
Where this goes wrong in practice. HFA is the control most sensitive to human factors, which is exactly why the failures are behavioural rather than technical.

items: The threshold is set where prompts are constant. A step-up that fires on every operation is satisfied reflexively within a week, and reflexive satisfaction is indistinguishable from no control.

A required factor cannot be presented. Social-login users have no password, so a password requirement is unsatisfiable rather than strict, and the failure looks like a bug rather than a policy choice.
Clients do not prefetch the policy. Without reading the effective policy first, the interface discovers the requirement by failing the send, which trains users to retry rather than to authenticate.
Denials are not monitored. human_factor_auth.denied is the signal that something is repeatedly attempting to move funds without a person, and it is worth an alert rather than a dashboard.

blocks.text: Sustained denials are more interesting than sustained approvals. Approval means the system is being used; denial means something is trying and failing, which is either a broken client or an attacker.

blocks.situation: You set the HFA policy to require a password for treasury sends. A batch of users, all of whom signed up through Google, immediately cannot send at all.
blocks.question: What happened?

options.text: Their sessions predate the policy and need re-issuing.
options.feedback: Policy changes take effect on the next protected call, so a stale session would surface as a prompt rather than an impossibility.

options.text: Social-login users have no password to verify, so the step-up cannot be satisfied at all.
options.feedback: Correct. There is nothing to check, so the requirement is unsatisfiable rather than merely inconvenient. Those users need a passkey or TOTP enrolled, or the policy should require a method they can actually present.

options.text: Google OAuth sessions are not eligible for step-up authentication.
options.feedback: They are eligible; the mechanism works for any authenticated user. The gap is the specific factor you chose, not the login method.

options.text: The policy resolved to the wallet spend policy instead of the user policy.
options.feedback: Resolution runs user policy first, then wallet, then defaults, so the user policy is what applied. It applied correctly and the requirement is the problem.

quiz.question: In what order does an HFA policy resolve?
options: User policy, then wallet spend policy, then defaults
Defaults, then wallet policy, then user policy
quiz.explanation: Resolution runs most specific first: the user's human_factor_auth_policies, then human_factor_auth on the wallet spend policy, then system defaults.

quiz.question: Why prefetch GET /v1/treasury/wallets/auth-policy?
options: So the client knows which step-up to prompt for before the user acts
quiz.explanation: Prefetching the effective policy lets the client show the right passkey or password prompt up front, instead of failing the send and retrying.

quiz.question: A social-login user has no password set. What breaks if the HFA policy requires the password method?
options: Nothing: a password is generated for them
The policy silently falls back to no step-up
They cannot satisfy the step-up until they enrol a passkey or TOTP
quiz.explanation: Without a password there is nothing to verify. They need to enrol a passkey or TOTP at /settings/security, or the policy should require one of those methods instead.

title: OIDC federation and Sign in with 1Claw
summary: Let external systems verify 1Claw-issued JWTs directly, so you can drop static API keys at the boundary.

blocks.text: 1Claw publishes a standard OpenID Connect issuer at https://api.1claw.co. That means an external relying party (Anthropic Workload Identity Federation, GCP STS, AWS STS) can validate a 1Claw-issued token against public keys instead of holding a long-lived shared secret.

items: GET /.well-known/openid-configuration: the issuer metadata.
GET /.well-known/jwks.json: the public signing keys.
Agent JWTs are signed EdDSA; federation tokens are RS256 from an HSM-backed RSA-2048 KMS key.
Each active key version publishes under a deterministic kid: eddsa-vN and rs256-vN.

blocks.text: Federation is deny-by-default. An agent has federation_enabled false until you turn it on, and federation_audiences is an allowlist where empty means deny everything.

steps.text: Read the issuer metadata. No auth required; this is what the relying party fetches.
Enable federation on the agent and allowlist exactly one audience.
Exchange the agent credential for a federated token using RFC 8693 token exchange.
Present the resulting RS256 JWT to the external service, which validates it against the JWKS.

blocks.text: TTL defaults to 900 seconds and is hard-capped at 3600. That cap is the point: a federated token is meant to be short-lived, unlike the static key it replaces.

Separately, 1Claw can act as an OAuth2 authorization server, "Sign in with 1Claw", with PKCE-required authorize, token, and userinfo endpoints under /v1/oauth. That is for signing users into your app, whereas federation is for machine identity at a service boundary.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Federation removes a static credential and replaces it with a validation contract, and the failures are all in the validation half.

items: The audience is not checked. A signature proves the issuer, not the intended recipient, and any customer of the same issuer can mint a validly signed token. Checking aud is what makes federation safe rather than merely convenient.
A kid is pinned. Pinning one key from the JWKS works until rotation, then fails everywhere at once, at a moment nobody connects to a key rotation.
The audience allowlist is left empty and assumed permissive. Empty means deny all, which is the safe default and the opposite of what people assume when a call unexpectedly fails.
Clock skew is not tolerated. Short TTLs make exp checks tight, and a relying party with a fast clock rejects tokens that are minutes from being issued.
The JWKS is fetched per request. It is stable and cacheable, and fetching it on every call turns the issuer into a hard dependency of your request path.

blocks.text: Short TTLs are the point and they raise the cost of every other mistake. A skew bug that would be invisible with a 24-hour token is an outage with a 900-second one.

blocks.situation: A partner wants to call your service using a 1Claw-issued federated token. They ask you to accept any token that validates against the 1Claw JWKS, since that proves it came from 1Claw.
blocks.question: Is that sufficient?

options.text: Yes. A valid signature from the published JWKS is exactly the guarantee federation provides.
options.feedback: It proves the issuer, which is necessary and not sufficient. Any 1Claw customer can mint a validly signed token; without checking who it was minted for, you accept tokens intended for someone else.

options.text: No. You must also validate the audience, or you will accept tokens minted for a different relying party.
options.feedback: Correct, and this is the classic confused-deputy shape. The agent's federation_audiences allowlist controls what it may request; your service must independently check that aud names you.

options.text: No. Federated tokens are RS256 and you should require EdDSA.
options.feedback: Backwards. Agent JWTs are EdDSA; federation tokens are deliberately RS256 because external relying parties overwhelmingly expect RSA. The algorithm is not the gap.

options.text: Yes, provided you pin a single kid from the JWKS.
options.feedback: Pinning a kid breaks silently on key rotation and still does not tell you who the token was issued for. It adds fragility without adding the missing check.

quiz.question: What does OIDC federation let you remove?
options: Static long-lived API keys at the service boundary
quiz.explanation: The relying party validates a short-lived 1Claw-issued JWT against published JWKS, so there is no long-lived shared secret to store or rotate.

quiz.question: An agent has federation_enabled true but federation_audiences empty. What happens?
options: The agent cannot authenticate at all
Only the default audience is allowed
quiz.explanation: federation_audiences is an allowlist and empty means deny all. Federation is deny-by-default throughout.

quiz.question: Which algorithms sign agent JWTs and federation tokens?
options: EdDSA for agent JWTs, RS256 for federation tokens
quiz.explanation: Agent JWTs use the EC_SIGN_ED25519 key (EdDSA); federation tokens use an HSM-backed RSA-2048 key (RS256), because external relying parties overwhelmingly expect RSA.

concepts.note: JWKS, audience binding, and short expiry

title: Lab: check what a real federated token would need to pass
summary: Use 1Claw's real issuer and real JWKS to write the audience check the federation lesson described, against the actual production values rather than invented ones.

blocks.text: The security-foundations JWKS lab showed you two real keys. This lab uses them for something: writing the exact verification a relying party would run on a 1Claw federation token, against the real issuer this course has been citing throughout.

steps.text: Confirm the real values this check depends on.
steps.code:
curl -s https://api.1claw.co/.well-known/openid-configuration | python3 -c '
import json, sys
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
print("issuer:  ", d["issuer"])
print("jwks_uri:", d["jwks_uri"])
'

steps.text: Both match what every lesson in this course has assumed without you checking.

Write the check a relying party actually runs: does a token's iss match this issuer, and does its aud match this service. Use a token shaped like a real federated one, since 1Claw will not hand you a live signed one without an account.
Both rejected, for different reasons, against the real issuer this course has cited every time.
steps.code:
REJECT: aud is https://billing.example.com, not https://deploy.example.com
REJECT: iss is https://api.1claw.io, not https://api.1claw.co

blocks.text: The second rejection is the one worth reading twice. api.1claw.io is not api.1claw.co, and it is exactly the kind of difference an inattentive check misses. Hardcoding the real issuer, confirmed live rather than copied from a lesson, is what makes that check meaningful rather than decorative.

items: This is the read-a-jwt lab's replay attack, run against 1Claw's actual issuer value instead of a placeholder. The mechanism does not change; using the real value is what makes it a check on the real system rather than a story about one.

The federation lesson's RFC 8693 token exchange exists to produce exactly the audience-bound token this check is written for. The exchange sets aud to whatever the relying party requested, so the relying party validating it is closing the loop it opened.

You cannot get a real, live, validly-signed federation token here without an account and an enabled agent. What you can do, and just did, is confirm the two facts, issuer and key location, that a correct implementation depends on getting right.

blocks.text: federation_audiences on the agent side is an allowlist of what a token may be requested for. This check is the other half, on the relying party's side: verifying that what arrived matches what you specifically asked for. Both halves are required; either alone is incomplete.

If you build a relying party for federated 1Claw tokens, do not hardcode the issuer string into your code from a lesson you read once. Fetch it from the discovery document at startup, the way this lab just did, so a future change is picked up rather than silently mismatched.

quiz.question: Why does the check reject a token with iss set to api.1claw.io?
options: It is a typo the parser cannot handle
It is a different issuer than the one confirmed live, and the check correctly treats it as untrusted
io domains are blocked by policy
quiz.explanation: A single-character domain difference is precisely what a careless implementation would miss. The check works because it compares against a confirmed real value rather than assuming.

quiz.question: Why is a token with a correct issuer but the wrong audience still rejected?
options: The signature does not cover aud
It proves the issuer signed it, not that it was meant for this service; any customer of that issuer could hold a validly issued token for somewhere else
quiz.explanation: This is the confused-deputy shape from earlier in the course. A real, validly signed token is not sufficient on its own; it has to be checked against who it was actually issued for.

quiz.question: Why fetch the issuer from the discovery document at runtime instead of hardcoding it from a lesson?
options: Discovery documents are faster to parse
It reduces the number of HTTP calls
A hardcoded value from a source read once will not pick up a future change, while fetching it keeps the check current
Hardcoding is against the OIDC spec
quiz.explanation: The whole point of a discovery document is that relying parties do not need to track issuer details out of band. Hardcoding a copied value defeats that and reintroduces the staleness risk this lab is about avoiding.
